editions.title: Midterm shockwaves hit AI and chip stocks; China reportedly blocks SoftBank-ABB deal
editions.notification: Democrats' midterm sweep rattles AI and chip stocks, and China reportedly blocks SoftBank's ABB robotics bid.
editions.intro:
The Democratic sweep of the US midterms dominated the day's tech news. Asian chip stocks slid, with South Korea's Kospi falling as much as 4.67% before a trading halt, and Samsung and SK hynix under pressure. Investors fear a Democrat-led Congress could tighten rules on AI data centres and scrutinise Trump-era AI and crypto trades. US markets recovered on Tuesday, with Nvidia up 2.3%, after the Nasdaq had briefly entered correction territory. Data centres were a clear election issue: an NBC exit poll found almost 80% of respondents opposed them in their neighbourhoods, and local measures restricting construction passed almost everywhere. Musk's record spending of around $450m for Republicans largely failed, and his companies now face likely tougher scrutiny.

Corporate news was mixed. AMD posted a record quarter, with revenue of $13.4bn and data centre making up about 63% of sales, and forecast $17bn next quarter, though its gaming business fell 40%. Apple shares dropped after it warned of thinner margins from higher memory costs. Uber reported strong third-quarter bookings of $59.8bn, but Waymo pulled out of its app in Austin and Atlanta the same day. In Europe and Asia, China reportedly blocked SoftBank's $5.4bn purchase of ABB's robotics unit, an FT report that is not yet confirmed.

Elsewhere, Google will switch off its AI features by default for K-12 student accounts, a move that drew criticism from New York's mayor. Cyber-attacks on European cold storage, including France's blood service, continued, with no group claiming responsibility. Anthropic and OpenAI both announced product and policy updates, including new image watermarking for older Claude models and animated GIF generation in ChatGPT.

top_stories.title: Kospi and chip stocks slump after Democratic midterm sweep
top_stories.summary: South Korean shares fell sharply, with the Kospi down as much as 4.67% and a temporary programme trading halt. Samsung and SK hynix led the drop on fears of tighter US rules on AI data centres.

top_stories.title: Data centres become a midterm issue and a possible regulatory clash
top_stories.summary: Exit polls showed strong opposition to data centres, and local measures restricting them passed in several states. Construction moratoriums and grid-cost rules are likely next, with Goldman Sachs flagging possible delays in Georgia and Texas.

top_stories.title: Local data centre measures largely voted down across the US
top_stories.summary: Of about 40 local measures, only one favoured expansion. Six outright bans passed, and two mayors were recalled over data centre disputes, signalling more scrutiny ahead.

top_stories.title: US tech stocks recover after AI spending selloff
top_stories.summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq rose on Tuesday after a brief slide that pushed the Nasdaq into correction. Nvidia gained 2.3% while Apple fell 1.9% on a weaker margin forecast.

top_stories.title: AMD posts record quarter on data centre demand
top_stories.summary: AMD reported record revenue of $13.4bn, with data centre at about 63% of sales. It forecasts $17bn next quarter and over 80% growth in 2027, though gaming revenue fell 40%.

top_stories.title: China reportedly blocks SoftBank's ABB robotics deal
top_stories.summary: The FT reports China's state planner opposed SoftBank's $5.4bn purchase of ABB's robotics arm. The report is unconfirmed, and SoftBank is weighing whether to seek approval again.

top_stories.summary: Google will turn off Gemini and AI features by default for K-12 accounts, and schools that keep AI disabled will lose Search access. The move reverses an August decision and drew criticism from New York's mayor.

editions.title: Fridge hacks spread across Europe as AMD posts record quarter
editions.notification: Supermarket fridges hacked across Europe, while AMD reports its best quarter ever.
editions.intro:
A suspected cyber-attack is spreading across Europe. Supermarket chains in at least seven countries, including Ahold Delhaize, Ikea, Carrefour Belgium and Colruyt, reported freezer temperatures rising overnight to as high as 50C, and some stores pulled chilled and frozen goods from sale. The EU food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain, and experts warned that many refrigeration controllers are reachable online and unpatched. It follows a French attack last month that affected hundreds of supermarkets. The UK's AI minister said a serious cyber breach is "extremely likely", and the NCSC warned that British firms were wilfully blind to threats.

In markets, the story was chipmakers. AMD reported a record $13.4 billion quarter, with data centre revenue of $8.5 billion, and guided to about $17 billion next quarter, while Intel guided to $15-16 billion. Its shares rose about 5% after hours, and analysts see AMD possibly overtaking Intel as the largest x86 chip vendor. AMD's gaming revenue fell 40%, however, as memory shortages driven by AI demand squeeze consumer hardware. Apple also reported a record iPhone quarter of $57.58 billion, up 17%, despite no standard iPhone launch, though it warned of higher memory costs.

Political and market backdrop was volatile. Democrats swept key US midterm races, including Texas, and European and Asian tech shares fell on expectations of tougher scrutiny of Trump-era policies. US tech stocks recovered on Tuesday after the Nasdaq had entered correction territory on Monday. Oracle reportedly dropped a $7 billion Tencent AI deal under US pressure, a single-source report that is worth watching.

top_stories.title: Democratic win rattles Trump-linked trades

top_stories.summary: HP and Asus are moving some PC manufacturing from Thailand and Vietnam back to China, with Dell reportedly considering it too. Rising memory and processor costs, and IDC's 20.1% fall in Q3 PC shipments, are driving the shift.

top_stories.summary: Drax has agreed a deal with Brookfield and Radiant for a datacentre at its North Yorkshire site, with potential investment above £20bn and eventual capacity over 1GW. Drax's market value rose almost 9%.

top_stories.summary: Gemini and other AI features will be off by default for K-12 student accounts, and schools that keep AI disabled will lose access to Google Search. The move reverses an August decision and drew criticism from New York's mayor.

editions.title: Apple beats on iPhone as Anthropic's compute bill tops $1trn
editions.notification: Apple's iPhone sales hit a record without a standard iPhone. Anthropic's compute commitments near $1trn. Read the briefing.
editions.intro:
Apple dominated the day's financial news. Its fourth-quarter results showed iPhone revenue of $57.58bn, up 17% year on year, driven by the pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and by price rises on older models. Total revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn, services reached $31.57bn and the Mac grew 24%, while iPad fell 10%. Chief executive John Ternus said memory costs were rising but partly offset. The foldable iPhone Duo, priced at $1,999, sold out quickly, and Apple said supply will be hard to predict. Apple's results are reported in the quarter to September, and its first full report under Ternus is due on 2 November.

The AI sector drew attention too. Anthropic's revised IPO filing shows roughly $895bn of compute and infrastructure commitments, which could top $1trn with other obligations. Revenue for the nine months to September reached $33.2bn, but the company warns that such rapid growth is unlikely to continue, and only about $213bn of the commitments can be avoided. Separately, the Financial Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia has told cloud partners to reduce exposure to Chinese clients, a move Nvidia has not confirmed. Palantir also reported a strong quarter, with US commercial revenue overtaking US government revenue for the first time, though its shares fell 3.1% before volatile after-hours trading.

Elsewhere, SpaceX is reportedly eyeing a purchase of Boost Mobile from EchoStar to gain tower access for Starlink phone service, though carriers have reportedly rejected earlier approaches. Across Europe, supermarket fridges and freezers were hit by a suspected cyber-attack spreading to at least seven countries, and Meta delayed new business terms after pushback over web scraping. Samsung retained the top smartphone spot in the third quarter as the overall market shrank 20%.

top_stories.title: Apple posts record iPhone quarter without a standard iPhone
top_stories.summary: Apple's quarterly iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.58bn, driven by the iPhone 18 Pro range and price rises on older models. Total revenue reached $114.5bn, with services at $31.57bn. Ternus said memory costs were partly offset by inventory and lower component costs.

top_stories.title: Anthropic's compute commitments could top $1trn

top_stories.summary: Supermarkets in at least seven countries reported fridge and freezer temperature spikes after suspected hacks. The attacks follow a French incident affecting hundreds of stores, and the EU food commissioner called them deliberate.

editions.title: Chip crunch deepens as Altman meets Samsung; Binance outflows
editions.notification: Memory chip shortage deepens as Sam Altman meets Samsung, and Binance users pull $3.6bn after its heist.
editions.intro:
The memory chip shortage dominated the last 24 hours. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman met roughly 50 Samsung executives at the company's Yongin site on Saturday, with Samsung confirming the talks covered how AI could reshape industries and business. No supply deals were announced, though memory supply is widely assumed to have been on the agenda. The meeting fits a wider pattern: Samsung and SK hynix are signing long-term customer agreements years ahead, with SK hynix saying its DRAM and HBM output is effectively sold out through 2029, yet both shares remain well below their 52-week highs.

Crypto was the other major theme. Binance users withdrew about $3.6bn as the exchange restarted services after a heist. The FBI and TRM Labs attribute the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, and Binance says it has found further breach points. Binance has pledged to reimburse users whose assets were stolen. Separately, French lawmakers voted narrowly to add a traffic-based levy on content providers to the 2027 budget. The amendment still has to clear further budget stages, and the government opposed it.

Elsewhere, Intel and AMD may be exploring cooperation, though neither has confirmed details. Spotify is reportedly preparing an AI product with a possible premium surcharge, and Apple's first results under CEO John Ternus are due on 2 November. Most other items are rumours or product news with limited near-term market impact.

top_stories.title: Altman meets Samsung as chip crunch deepens

editions.title: Amazon's AI spend, Microsoft buyouts and a neocloud wobble
editions.notification: Amazon's AWS grew 39% but free cash flow turned deeply negative. Here is why AI spending is squeezing Big Tech.
editions.intro:
Amazon dominated the period. Its third-quarter results showed Amazon Web Services growing 39% to $46bn, with a backlog of $578bn, but revenue and earnings per share came in slightly below forecasts and shares fell as much as 7% in extended trading. Free cash flow over the past year slipped to minus $42.4bn, largely from AI capital spending. Chief executive Andy Jassy said AWS should grow more than 40% in 2027 and 2028 and that Amazon will spend meaningfully more on AI next year.

The cash squeeze is a wider theme. A Reuters analysis of LSEG data finds that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle returned the smallest share of their cash to shareholders in at least 15 years, with buybacks down 83%. Their combined capital spending of $556.9bn exceeded operating cash flow, leaving a free cash flow deficit of $14bn. Meanwhile Microsoft is offering voluntary severance to about 60,000 staff while protecting AI-critical teams, and its AI infrastructure budget is about $170bn for 2026.

Doubts about the AI build-out are growing. Shares in neocloud firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have fallen by about a quarter in a month, and Nvidia quietly lowered published bandwidth targets for its Vera Rubin hardware. Reports also say OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10bn. Against that backdrop, Oracle shares rose about 14% during its AI World conference, though they remain well below their late 2025 high.

top_stories.title: AWS grows 39% but Amazon's cash burn deepens
top_stories.summary: Amazon posted record operating margins and a 39% jump in AWS revenue, but results were slightly below forecasts and shares fell sharply after hours. Free cash flow of minus $42.4bn shows how heavily AI spending is weighing on the business, and Jassy signalled more investment in 2027.

top_stories.title: Big Tech buybacks fall 83% as AI spending outruns cash
top_stories.summary: Five hyperscalers returned the smallest share of cash to shareholders in at least 15 years. Their capex exceeded operating cash flow, with the gap funded by reserves, borrowing and share sales, despite more than $3tn in AI commitments.

top_stories.title: Microsoft offers voluntary severance to a quarter of staff
top_stories.summary: Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 employees, excluding data centres, sales, cybersecurity and quantum teams. It is the second such programme this year and comes as it keeps AI infrastructure spending near $170bn.

top_stories.title: Neocloud shares slump as bubble fears grow
top_stories.summary: CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN and Applied Digital have lost about a quarter of their value in a month, weighed by heavy debt and rising borrowing costs. A Microsoft deal cancellation and lower spending forecasts have added to the unease.

top_stories.title: Nvidia quietly trims Vera Rubin bandwidth specs
top_stories.summary: Nvidia reduced published memory and interconnect bandwidth for Vera Rubin hardware without a press release. Analysts read it as a fallback after memory suppliers struggled to hit target speeds, which could help AMD's rival parts look better on paper.

top_stories.title: OpenAI reportedly cuts fundraising target by $10bn
top_stories.summary: According to the Financial Times, OpenAI is now seeking about $20bn at a valuation near $1.25tn, a reduction that is framed as tempering ambitions amid sector anxiety. Details are limited in the available summary.

top_stories.summary: The South China Morning Post reports Apple intends to launch AI features on iPhones in China in December through an Alibaba partnership. Scope, regulatory approval and terms are unclear, and Apple has not commented in the available text.

editions.title: DoorDash buys Instacart; tech sell-off deepens over AI spending
editions.notification: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for about $17bn as AI spending worries rattle tech stocks.
editions.intro:
The biggest development is DoorDash's agreed deal to buy rival Instacart at $65 a share, a 26% premium, valuing the business at roughly $17 billion. The cash-heavy offer still needs regulatory and shareholder approval, and it would leave iPhone users with one fewer app-based grocery and delivery option. The deal lands amid a sharp slide in US tech shares, with the Nasdaq posting its worst month since March 2025.

That selloff is driven by fears about the roughly $800 billion that Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon and Microsoft are committing to spending in 2026. Intel fell 28% after warning of weaker PC demand, while Reddit dropped 29% after weak user numbers and complaints that Google's AI search is cutting its referral traffic. Reddit's CEO said Google's AI Mode does not drive meaningful traffic, and Alphabet's core ad growth slowed to its weakest pace in five quarters even as it kept capex guidance of up to $205 billion.

The AI nervousness also shows up in private markets. The Financial Times reports that OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10 billion, citing the AI selloff and Anthropic's forthcoming listing; Anthropic's IPO filing, meanwhile, shows $16.3 billion of first-half revenue alongside heavy losses. Apple, by contrast, retook the title of the world's most valuable listed company, supported by iPhone demand and its China AI rollout.

top_stories.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for about $17bn
top_stories.summary: DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart at $65 a share, a 26% premium, with at least 75% cash consideration. The deal still needs approval and would remove one grocery delivery option for iPhone users.

top_stories.title: US tech shares slump as AI spending nears $1tn
top_stories.summary: Intel fell 28% after warning of weaker PC demand, Reddit dropped 29% and Alphabet slid further. The Nasdaq had its worst month since March 2025 as investors question heavy AI capital spending.

top_stories.title: OpenAI trims fundraising target by $10bn
top_stories.summary: The FT reports OpenAI has cut its target amid an AI stock selloff and Anthropic's upcoming listing. The move could shape private AI valuations and investor appetite ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

top_stories.title: Reddit's CEO says Google's AI Mode does not drive traffic
top_stories.summary: Reddit reported search referrals fell by over a million a week in October and blamed AI Overviews and AI Mode. Reddit is also requiring logins and pushing new AI-driven feeds.

top_stories.title: Apple Intelligence to reach China in December
top_stories.summary: Apple confirmed its AI features will launch in mainland China with iOS 27.3, with Alibaba's Qwen supporting some experiences. The Siri AI rebuild is not included in the launch.

top_stories.title: Murata to spend $6.4bn doubling AI capacitor output
top_stories.summary: Murata will invest ¥1 trillion over five years to more than double MLCC sales, citing unprecedented demand from AI data centres. Its September-quarter profit beat analyst estimates by a wide margin.

top_stories.title: Apple reclaims most valuable company crown
top_stories.summary: Apple has overtaken Nvidia again as the world's most valuable listed company, closing at $344.63 on 30 October. The lead has swung between the two as iPhone demand competes with AI chip demand.

LiveWire warns of going-concern doubt, withdraws guidance and shares fall over 40%; a restructuring committee is exploring options.
GM agrees to pay $220m to 36 attorneys general over sale of driver data to brokers and insurers.
Meta settles a social media addiction case days before a Los Angeles trial; Snap remains the only defendant.
A WAP Push SMS flaw can disable Android 12+ phones; a fix is in the October patch for Android 14 and later only.
Anthropic denies any link between its systems and a tampered Claude Code extension that reached up to 5,000 developers via Cursor.

Finance.title: Democrats win Congress; markets weigh gridlock and AI risk
Finance.notification: Democrats take both chambers of Congress, and markets are weighing gridlock against AI risk.
Finance.summary:
Democrats have won control of both the US House and Senate in the 3 November midterms, ending Trump's full control of Congress for the rest of his second term. Economists expect two years of gridlock, since Trump keeps veto power and Democrats lack a filibuster-proof Senate majority. Stocks and the dollar fell on the result before recovering in some markets, while the AI trade was hit hardest, with chipmakers in Asia and US tech stocks under pressure. Voters also rejected local data centre projects on the ballot.

Across the UK and Europe, the focus is on rates and living costs. The Bank of England is widely expected to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on Thursday, its first rise since August 2023, after CPI reached 3.5%. Eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, and the ECB race to succeed Christine Lagarde has begun. In Asia, Japanese and Korean shares fell on AI worries, while China moved to slow the yuan's rally.

Oil, with Brent near or above $100 earlier in the week, remains sensitive to US-Iran talks and Gulf shipping risks.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and economists expect gridlock. Stocks fell on the news before some rallied, with AI and data centre concerns weighing.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: The Bank of England is widely expected to lift Bank Rate to 4% on Thursday, its first rise since 2023, as CPI reached 3.5%.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: Eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, a three-year high, driven by energy. The race to succeed Lagarde at the ECB has formally begun.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Kospi and Nikkei fell on AI scrutiny fears, while China raised the FX reserve requirement to slow the yuan's rally.

highlights.label: Markets
highlights.text: Brent fell sharply after the US vote, but remains sensitive to US-Iran talks and Gulf shipping threats.

points.text: Democrats can now subpoena and block Cabinet nominees, but Trump keeps the veto and Trump's $5,000 payment pledge looks unlikely.
Voters approved nearly every data centre moratorium or restriction on the ballot across at least 40 US jurisdictions.
Apple reports its first quarter under CEO John Ternus, with investors focused on rising memory-chip costs and the iPhone outlook.
Anthropic returned to an operating loss in Q3 and faces $895bn of compute commitments as its Nasdaq listing nears.
Big Tech AI bond sales could push up borrowing costs in Europe, with France's 10-year yield near 5%.
Governments have until 6 November to nominate ECB candidates; Lagarde leaves on 7 February 2027.

World.title: Democrats seize Congress as midterm results reshape Washington
World.notification: Democrats take the Senate and look set for the House, as Trump says he will work with them.
World.summary:
Democrats have won control of the US Senate and are projected to take the House in the 3 November midterms, a result that gives them a check on President Donald Trump for the last two years of his term. Key wins include Texas, Maine, Kansas, Iowa and North Carolina, and voters reportedly cited living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran, which has pushed up fuel prices. Trump said the vote was not about him and that he would accept the results, while also warning he could veto legislation he considers insane.

For markets, the political shift matters mainly through its effect on the Iran conflict and energy. Oil fell for a fourth session on hopes of lower escalation risk, and Brent dropped sharply in recent sessions, while US stocks rallied after the vote. Traders will watch whether a divided Washington constrains tariffs, defence spending and Iran policy.

Elsewhere, US strikes on Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz and reports of Iranian guerrilla tactics there underline that the energy risk is not yet resolved. In Europe and Asia, the Ukraine peace track and Hong Kong's national security cases also drew attention.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Democrats won the Senate and are projected to take the House, with Trump saying he will work with them while threatening vetoes.

highlights.label: Iran and oil
highlights.text: US strikes near Qeshm Island and reports of Iranian guerrilla tactics in Hormuz keep energy risk high, even as oil fell for four days.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: The UK agreed to time-bound talks on the slave trade, with a formal apology possible by the G20 in Manchester next November.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: Spain's transport minister will resign after a train crash killed 69 people, while France prepares a nationwide strike over cost of living and cuts.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion, drawing criticism from Human Rights Watch and Amnesty.

highlights.label: Markets
highlights.text: Indian stocks jumped to near three-month highs as Brent crude slid about 10% in recent sessions after the US vote.

points.text: Troy Jackson is projected to have beaten Republican Susan Collins in Maine, the only GOP senator in a state Trump lost in 2024.
Democrat Josh Turek flipped Iowa's Senate seat, which Republicans had held and no Democrat had won in over a decade.
House Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek the House minority leader post after the Republican losses.
At least 26 people were killed in a Russian strike on a school in Zaporizhzhia, derailing hopes for progress on peace.
Zelenskyy hopes the Democratic Congress will bring more US help; Abu Dhabi talks are set for 10 and 11 November.
Israel's opposition leaders backed Gadi Eisenkot to replace Netanyahu, though no bloc has a Knesset majority.

Tech.title: Cyber-attacks on fridges and AI backlash dominate tech
Tech.notification: Supermarket fridges across Europe hit by suspected cyber-attacks, with temperatures reportedly reaching 50C.
Tech.summary:
A wave of suspected cyber-attacks on refrigeration systems is the day's most serious story. Supermarkets in at least seven European countries, including Ahold Delhaize, Ikea and Carrefour Belgium, reported fridge and freezer temperatures rising overnight to as high as 50C, and some shops pulled chilled and frozen goods from sale. France's national blood service said hackers also tampered with cold stores, though no blood was lost. No group has claimed responsibility, and the EU food commissioner has called the attacks a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.

Politics is shaping the tech mood too. A Democratic sweep of Congress unsettled markets, with Asian chip shares and Korea's Kospi falling sharply, and the Nasdaq entered a correction on Monday before recovering on Tuesday. Opposition to AI data centres emerged as a political issue, with local measures restricting construction passing across the US and Musk's midterm spending widely seen as a setback.

Corporate news was led by strong AI-driven results. AMD reported a record quarter, with data centre revenue up sharply, while Apple posted record iPhone revenue despite no standard iPhone launch. Meanwhile, Canva is cutting or relocating 22% of its workforce, and Waymo has ended its exclusive Uber tie-up in Austin and Atlanta.

highlights.label: Apple
highlights.text: iPhone revenue hit $57.58bn, up 17%, driven by the pricier iPhone 18 Pro models. Total revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn.

highlights.label: AMD
highlights.text: Record Q3 revenue of $13.4bn, with data centre sales of $8.5bn. Guidance points to $17bn next quarter.

highlights.label: Data centres
highlights.text: Local ballot measures largely restricted new data centre construction, with six outright bans passing.

highlights.label: Canva
highlights.text: The design firm is cutting or relocating 1,271 staff, 22% of its global workforce, in a major restructure.

highlights.label: Robotaxis
highlights.text: Waymo stopped letting Uber users book its robotaxis in Austin and Atlanta, the same day Uber reported 20% bookings growth.

points.text: Google will switch off Gemini and Search AI features for K-12 students until schools opt in, drawing criticism from NYC's mayor.
Geoffrey Hinton warned AI could trigger a large-scale blackout later this year or next, and backed mandatory independent testing.

HP and Asus are reportedly moving some PC production back to China as memory costs push up component prices.
Apple has told employees and contractors not to use insider information to bet in prediction markets.
AI inference startup Fal raised $1.3bn at a $16bn valuation, double its April figure, with Nvidia taking part.

Fashion.title: Estée Lauder lifts outlook as fragrance drives turnaround
Fashion.notification: Estée Lauder raises its forecast as fragrance surges 20%, while Coty and Burberry show the sector's uneven recovery.
Fashion.summary:
Estée Lauder Companies delivered a strong first quarter, with organic sales up 6% and an adjusted operating margin of 12.1%, up from 7.3%. Fragrance led the way, rising 20% on the back of Le Labo, Tom Ford, Jo Malone London and Kilian Paris, and the group raised its fiscal 2027 growth forecast to 4-5.5%. Chief executive Stéphane de La Faverie said spending on consumer-facing marketing will rise as the turnaround continues.

The wider beauty and fashion picture is more mixed. Coty reported a 1% sales decline and called fiscal 2027 a transition year with an uneven recovery, though it extended the Marc Jacobs licence for 40 years and cut net debt by more than $300 million. Burberry's chief executive Joshua Schulman said the Burberry Forward turnaround is continuing despite difficult markets, while Hugo Boss lowered its outlook on weak demand and higher costs.

Political and economic backdrop matters too. US midterm results, which handed Democrats control of Congress, were followed by a sharp rise in the Dow, and Vogue Business notes that affordability concerns and near-record low consumer sentiment still weigh on luxury buyers. Several groups still cite the US as a bright spot, and the CFDA Awards in New York highlighted the industry's creative side.

highlights.label: Hugo Boss
highlights.text: Hugo Boss cut its annual outlook, citing weaker consumer demand and higher costs. The revised figures were not in the feed summary.

highlights.label: Burberry
highlights.text: CEO Joshua Schulman says the Burberry Forward turnaround continues, with Burberry House on Regent Street and a Shanghai exhibition marking the 170th anniversary.

highlights.label: Coty
highlights.text: Coty's sales fell 1% and it extended the Marc Jacobs licence for 40 years, while calling FY27 a transition year.

highlights.label: CFDA Awards
highlights.text: Anthony Vaccarello was named International Designer of the Year for his decade at Saint Laurent, with Peter Marino receiving the Fashion Icon Award.

highlights.label: Louis Vuitton
highlights.text: The 2026 holiday campaign is built around train travel, linking to Nicolas Ghesquière's fall 2025 show and LVMH's Orient Express partnership.

highlights.label: Hong Kong
highlights.text: Hong Kong jewellery and watch sales rose 22% in the first nine months as wealthy buyers turned to gold, while China's luxury market slows.

points.text: Estée Lauder has set medium-term 2030 growth and margin targets, though the specific figures were not in the summary.
Palace and Burberry have released a 10-piece capsule to mark Palace's London flagship opening on 5 November.

A Cold Wall has named Joshua A. Bullen as its first designer in residence, with a debut planned in Paris for fall 2027.
The founders of Paris label Coperni have shut the brand down, according to Business of Fashion; reasons were not given.
